summary:
Slovakia presents no entry or documentation obstacle specific to a trans visitor. Movement into and residence in the country falls under European Union free-movement rules. Under the Court of Justice of the European Union's Coman ruling of 5 June 2018, couples resident in Slovakia who married in an EU state where one partner holds EU citizenship enjoy full residency rights, and the Interior Ministry announced immediate compliance.

Legal gender recognition exists in principle but the procedure is medicalised and restrictive. In practice surgical sterilisation has usually been required before identity documents can be amended, and registry offices are refusing to process gender-change applications pending new standards. The Ministry of Health's standards of care were revoked on 18 May 2022 under pressure from the Conference of Slovak Bishops and legislators, leaving no valid standards; by 18 November 2022 healthcare providers were refusing transgender care, forcing people to seek treatment abroad. Standards were republished on 3 March 2023, but their implementation in care access and civil registries remains to be seen. A guideline that had permitted document change without surgery was revoked on 21 November 2023 on grounds of government coalition stability.

Legislative attempts to criminalise trans lives have recurred. Bills tabled by ĽSNS on 12 February 2021 and by the Republic Movement on 23 September 2021 and again on 13 January 2023 sought to ban legal gender change and, in the 2023 version, to outlaw medical transition with a prison sentence of at least four years. All failed, mostly on abstentions. A separate bill of 24 February 2023 restricting legal gender change to people whose sex was 'wrongly assigned at birth', provable only by a karyotype test, passed first reading with 87 votes.

Hate-crime and anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation more explicitly than gender identity. A Criminal Code amendment of May 2013 added sexual orientation as a hate-crime ground carrying harsher penalties and outlawed hate speech on that basis. The Anti-Discrimination Act, adopted in 2004 to meet EU requirements and broadened in 2008, outlaws discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity across employment, education, housing, social care and the provision of goods and services, and applies to the military, where LGBT people serve openly; a 2005 Pravda report described a 'very homophobic environment' in the armed forces.

Violence against LGBT venues has been lethal. On 12 October 2022 a 19-year-old attacker whose primary target was then-prime minister Eduard Heger, with the Bratislava LGBT bar Tepláreň as a fallback, arrived about 18:35 and at 19:11 fired eight shots at the bar, killing two people and injuring one; the perpetrator also died. Rights groups described the attack as marking a new era for trans people in the country, and the aftermath brought greater fear about the future. In an April 2023 letter to the National Council, Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Dunja Mijatović wrote that six months after the attack there was no discernible progress, that the human rights of LGBTI people appeared more, not less, at risk, and that she was concerned by regressive legislative proposals including the legal-gender-recognition ban bill.

Official hostility has come from within government. On 3 July 2024 the serving Minister of Culture, Martina Šimkovičová, made a public homophobic and racist statement claiming Europe is dying because of an excessive number of LGBT people.

Partner recognition is narrow. Slovakia recognises no civil unions or same-sex marriage; bills introduced in 1997, 2000, 2012, 2018, 2021 and 2022 were all rejected, including 94 votes against to 14 for in 2012, 31 of 150 in support in 2018, and 7 for against 67 against in 2021. A constitutional amendment of June 2014 (Article 41) defining marriage as 'a unique union between a man and a woman' passed 102 to 18, potentially rendering future recognition laws unconstitutional. Any existing marriage is invalidated on change of legal gender, and as of 2025 only married couples may adopt, barring same-sex couples, single people and unmarried partners. Since 1964 the law recognises only a 'close person', a sibling or spouse, with limited rights, mainly inheritance. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship should expect no recognition of that relationship under Slovak law.

The wider climate is hostile by EU standards. Slovakia is described as having some of the worst LGBTQ rights in the European Union and less supportive public opinion than the Czech Republic. Support is volatile: 66% acceptance in a 2007 Pew survey, 29 to 57% backing civil unions in 2019, falling to 40% after the 2022 attack; the 2015 Eurobarometer put Slovakia fourth-lowest in the EU on same-sex marriage at 24%, and PlanetRomeo's 2015 Gay Happiness Index ranked Slovakia 47th against Czechia's 18th. The gay scene is small, consisting of a few bars and clubs in Bratislava.
tangentialFactors:
Public-order friction around LGBT events has a documented history. Slovakia's first gay Pride, held in Bratislava on 22 May 2010, drew about a thousand attendees confronted by right-wing groups who threw stones at speakers, dispersed tear gas and infiltrated the march, forcing cancellation of the city-centre route; 29 people were arrested.

Referendum politics have repeatedly put LGBT questions to the electorate. The Alliance for the Family's 2014 petition demanded a ban on same-sex adoption, the prohibition of sex education in schools and a referendum question barring schools from requiring children to take sexual-behaviour education. The third question was ruled unconstitutional, and the referendum of 7 February 2015 on the remaining questions was invalid at 21.07% turnout after opponents urged a boycott.

Regional comparison is unfavourable. Slovakia is ranked below the Czech Republic on public support and on the 2015 Gay Happiness Index, and the 2015 Eurobarometer placed it fourth-lowest in the EU on same-sex marriage.
localsOnly:
Blood donation is restricted by sexual behaviour: gay and bisexual people are barred from donating if they had unprotected sex within the previous year.

A 2017 Iniciatíva Inakosť survey found nearly 40% of LGBT respondents had faced active discrimination, 15.2% in the previous year, with many reporting low self-esteem, anxiety, depression, alcohol abuse and suicidal feelings attributed to homophobic persecution; fewer than half were willing to hold a partner's hand in public.

The same survey recorded mixed reactions to disclosure within families: 54% of mothers, 42% of fathers and 49.5% of grandparents were accepting, while 28.5% of fathers and 29% of grandparents were indifferent.
outOfScopeNotes:
The fate of the 24 February 2023 bill after its first reading is not established by the sources reviewed.

Whether the standards of care republished on 3 March 2023 are being applied in registries and clinics, and whether registry offices continue to refuse gender-change applications, is unresolved.

An Amnesty International statement of May 2023 and a Pew Research Center survey on religion and minorities produced no usable finding for this record.
